newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jew, Arab in Hebron fearful as deal nears.
newsitem.headline: Jew, Arab in Hebron fearful as deal nears.

text.p: Jew and Arab in Hebron faced the new year with apprehension as Israel and the PLO neared a deal on the fate of the West Bank town.

"Whatever happens here there's an explosion. If Israel pulls out there's going to be an explosion and if Israel stays there's going to be an explosion," David Wilder, a spokesman for Hebron's 400 Jewish settlers, told Reuters.
Israel and Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority struggled on Tuesday to wrap up three months of talks on an Israeli handover of 80 percent of Hebron to PLO self-rule.
In Hebron itself, residents harboured no illusions the long-overdue deal would herald a new era of peace for the volatile West Bank town.

"What is this redeployment? I don't understand the meaning of the word redeployment," said Abu Samir al-Sharabati, a Palestinian merchant who lives in the 20 percent of Hebron due to remain under Israeli military control.
Sharabati said Israeli security forces trampled across his home and roof at dawn on Tuesday on their way to detain 15 Jewish settlers who tried to seize houses in the Arab casbah.
"Go ask the politicians what a 'pullout' is," he said.
Hebron, the traditional burial site of the biblical Abraham, is holy to Moslems and Jews and a bastion of militancy for both.
Wilder called the Hebron deal a "suicide pact" aimed at putting a stranglehold on the heavily fortified Jewish settler enclaves in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs.
He said the pre-dawn takeover of empty Arab houses on Tuesday was aimed at reclaiming Jewish property "stolen" by Palestinians and to prevent the housing of "terrorists" there.
"There are military intelligence documents that have revealed Arafat is planning on filling those homes with 600 terrorists who were released from Israeli jails," Wilder said.
Israeli soldiers clashed with settlers who last week tried to occupy two vacant houses in a similar action.
"This isn't the way the police should be acting," he said.

The settlers accuse Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's right-wing prime minister opposed to swapping occupied land for peace with the Arabs, of betraying them for sticking with the U.S.-backed deal signed by the left-leaning government he ousted in May.
The handover, due last March, was delayed by a wave of Islamist suicide bombings in Israel. It was pushed off further by Netanyahu's demands to bolster security for the city's Jews.
Palestinians say the partial handover is a step in the right direction but not sufficient to guarantee stability in the town.
"God willing, there will be peace in Hebron in the coming year," Palestinian journalist Hassan Riba'i said. "But real peace means removal of the settlers and the army from the city."

As proof the tomb could not remain under sole Israeli control, Riba'i cited a Jewish settler's massacre in 1994 of 29 Moslem worshippers at the Tomb of the Patriarchs, known to Moslems as al-Ibrahimi mosque.
"Haram al-Ibrahimi is a holy place to Moslems above all... only Palestinian police can guarantee Palestinian security," he said.
Arafat has demanded a Palestinian presence at the site. Netanyahu has rejected the idea. Israel Radio said the two would take up the issue at their next summit.
The town's Jews, who see Hebron and all the West Bank as parts of the biblical Land of Israel promised the Jews by God, insist they will not be budged.
"Any foothold that we give them above what they already have is pure stupidity," Wilder said. "The creator of the world didn't bring us back here to throw us out again."
Israeli army radio said the gunman was a young man who wore the skullcap of a religious Jew. Its report did not say the man was a soldier but that he had already been taken into custody.
The incident occurred just as Israel and the Palestinians neared a deal to hand over most of the West Bank town to Palestinian self-rule.
